title: K-19: The Widowmaker
full_review:
A rushed-into-service Russian submarine malfunctions in a way that could have worldwide catastrophic results in the fact-based Cold War drama, "K-19: The Widowmaker" (Paramount).

With Cold War tensions running high in 1961, the Soviets want their new flagship nuclear submarine, the K-19, sent on its maiden mission at once. Its captain, Mikhail Polenin (Liam Neeson), objects strongly that the unfinished sub is not ready and his crew would be endangered. Polenin is quickly demoted to executive officer and Captain Vostrikov (Harrison Ford) arrives, determined to meet all his superior's deadlines.

With nearly a dozen men already killed during construction, the jumpy crew has nicknamed the K-19 "the widowmaker." Matters get worse once they set sail as Vostrikov, an unforgiving taskmaster, stresses the crew to the max with constant, risky drills that leave him scornful of both crew and officers' performance. Polenin pleads for tolerance from the captain, to no avail.

En route to spy patrol an area between New York and Washington, officer Radtchenko (Peter Sarsgaard), the rookie in charge of the core reactor, realizes the cooling system has sprung a leak and the reactor is heating up. This could progress to a meltdown, setting off the missile warheads and likely starting World War III.

The sub lacks a back-up system or even radiation suits and the intensely radioactive reactor compartment must be opened to add distilled water and begin the cool-down process. Such a maneuver might not succeed but would surely spread deadly radiation levels throughout the sub.

Vostrikov and Polenin also clash over contacting a nearby NATO base and an American destroyer for humanitarian assistance, with the captain insistent on ignoring outsiders, even at the cost of his men's lives.

As directed by Kathryn Bigelow, this is a fact-inspired tale of courage, honor and duty. Unfortunately, it's not gripping. Ford is stiff in the role, grimly enunciating with a passable Russian accent, but never looking convincing or comfortable in his portrayal of the stoic sub commander. Faring much better is Neeson, who is quite credible as the sensitive former captain, but both characterizations are too cut and dried. Polenin is ever humane while Vostrikov is almost always cruel and inhuman. Such blunt, black-and-white stereotypes detract from the human drama of lives at risk and the larger political implications.

Ford scowls a great deal, except for his unexpected "May God be with you" to the first crew members entering the radioactive chamber. Another frightened sailor secretly wearing a crucifix is chastised by atheist Radtchenko, who later relents on seeing the man horribly burned by radiation exposure.

Despite its stodgy pacing, the film is fascinating for its revelation of a story, kept under cover by the Soviets for decades, that could have had disastrous global consequences.

Due to brief violence, images of injured seamen and fleeting rear nudity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
(
2002
)
